title: Fed Holds Rates Steady as Chair Warsh Signals Patience Amid Cooling Inflation
excerpt: June CPI posted its sharpest drop since the pandemic, but the new Fed chief warns against declaring 'mission accomplished' — and a divided FOMC keeps the door open to hikes later this year.
body:
• The Federal Reserve has held its benchmark rate at 3.50%–3.75% through two meetings under new Chair Kevin Warsh, and markets price an 85% chance of another hold on July 29.
  • June CPI fell to 3.5% year-over-year from 4.2% in May — the steepest monthly decline since the pandemic — while core CPI eased to 2.6%.
  • Warsh told Congress the Fed has "no tolerance" for elevated inflation but declined to signal whether a rate hike is coming, breaking with the forward-guidance tradition of his predecessor.
  • The June dot plot showed nine FOMC officials projecting at least one rate hike this year, with markets pricing a better-than-50% chance of a move by September.

The Federal Reserve enters its July 28–29 policy meeting on a knife-edge: inflation is cooling faster than almost anyone expected, yet the central bank's own projections and a chorus of hawkish officials suggest rate increases are still very much on the table.

At his first Congressional testimony as Fed chair on July 14–15, Kevin Warsh delivered a message that was resolute on inflation but deliberately opaque on the near-term rate path. "Inflation is a choice," Warsh told the House Financial Services Committee. "The members of our committee have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation, and we share a resolute commitment to restore price stability."

When pressed on whether the Fed would hike at its upcoming meeting, Warsh refused to tip his hand — a sharp departure from the forward-guidance playbook that defined the Jerome Powell era.

Why Rates Are on Hold

The case for patience got a significant boost on the morning of Warsh's testimony. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index fell 0.4% month-over-month in June — the first monthly decline since 2020 and roughly four times better than the -0.1% economists had forecast. Year-over-year CPI decelerated to 3.5%, down sharply from May's 4.2% reading and below the consensus estimate of 3.8%.

Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, was flat for the month at 0.0%, well below the 0.2% forecast. On an annual basis, core inflation fell to 2.6% from 2.9%, bringing the Fed's 2% target into closer reach for the first time since the Iran war disrupted energy markets in late February.

The decline was driven in large part by falling gasoline prices after crude oil pulled back from its Iran war highs. The Producer Price Index similarly retreated in June, though core wholesale inflation still registered a modest gain.

"There might be some that look at this morning's data and say, 'Oh, mission accomplished. Everything is swell.' That is not my view," Warsh said, cautioning lawmakers against over-reading a single month's print.

New York Fed President John Williams, a voting FOMC member, offered a more optimistic read, saying there are "encouraging reasons to expect that inflation has peaked and should edge down in coming quarters." Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he needed "several months" of softer readings before he would feel confident inflation was durably moving lower.

The Warsh Factor

Warsh, 55, took the helm in May after being nominated by President Trump late last year. A former Morgan Stanley investment banker and the youngest-ever Fed governor when he was first appointed to the board in 2006, Warsh is a known monetary hawk — but one who has so far governed with a deliberate air of unpredictability.

His most consequential policy shift has been the abandonment of forward guidance. Where Powell would carefully telegraph the Fed's likely direction weeks ahead of a meeting, Warsh has said that sharing "every passing thought" risks creating a feedback loop in which policymakers seek data to confirm their priors.

"It's a little tricky with Warsh coming in, because he's not necessarily going to give you the same guidance that past Fed leadership would have," said Jeremy Schwartz, senior U.S. economist at Nomura. "He hasn't given any indication that he's inclined to hike rates."

That silence has left markets to parse the signals from other officials. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan became the first policymaker to publicly advocate for higher rates this week, saying she "currently believe[s] modestly higher interest rates would better balance the outlook." Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack echoed the sentiment, citing businesses urging the Fed to act and consumers struggling with persistent price pressures.

In June, the Fed's updated dot plot showed a dramatic hawkish shift: nine officials penciled in at least one rate hike this year, and six projected more than one. Three months earlier, no officials had projected any hikes. Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economic research at Bank of America, estimated that five of the 12 voting FOMC members currently favor tightening.

Market Reaction

Markets have swung sharply on the interplay between cooling inflation data and hawkish Fed rhetoric. After the June CPI release, the probability of a July rate hike plummeted to roughly 16% from 40%, according to the CME FedWatch tool, while the odds of a hold jumped above 83%.

Equities rallied on the morning of the inflation print — Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 1.3% and S&P 500 futures rose 0.4% pre-market — but gave back gains over the rest of the week as Middle East tensions escalated. The S&P 500 closed at approximately 7,463 on Friday, down 1.6% for the week, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.9%.

The 10-year Treasury yield settled around 4.55%, roughly one basis point lower on the day but still elevated by recent standards. The U.S. dollar index held near 100.74. Brent crude surged to $87.75 a barrel on renewed U.S.–Iran military strikes, adding a fresh inflationary wild card ahead of the July meeting.

Traders in derivatives markets now see a better-than-50% chance of a rate hike at the September meeting, even as many economists expect the Fed to stay on hold through the year. Marc Giannoni, chief U.S. economist at Barclays, forecasts no change in rates through the end of 2027.

What It Means for NRI Investors

The rupee has slipped to around 94.74 per dollar, pressured by the dollar's strength as rate-hike expectations have repriced higher. A prolonged hold by the Fed would offer some relief to the currency, but the threat of hikes later this year keeps the depreciation bias intact.

For NRI investors with U.S. dollar-denominated holdings, the elevated rate environment continues to favour money-market funds and short-duration bonds, which are yielding well above 4%. Those with mortgage exposure should note that the 10-year yield — a key benchmark for U.S. home-loan rates — remains elevated and is unlikely to fall materially until the Fed's rate path becomes clearer.

Outlook

The FOMC's July 28–29 meeting is shaping up to be the most closely watched since the tightening cycle began in 2022. While a hold remains the strong consensus, the possibility of a hawkish surprise — or a dissent from one of the vocal hawks — cannot be ruled out.

"For Warsh, yelling about it but not hiking because inflation is coming down is the best of all worlds," said Guy LeBas, chief fixed-income strategist at Janney Montgomery Scott. Bank of America's Bhave expects Warsh to wait until September before raising rates, potentially delivering three hikes by year-end.

What happens next will depend on two variables: whether July's inflation data confirms the disinflationary trend, and whether the U.S.–Iran conflict drives another oil-price shock. If both break favourably, the Fed may have room to hold well into the autumn. If not, Warsh's promise to end elevated inflation "on my watch" could be tested sooner than markets expect.
